new_entities.name: IV high-dose vitamin C
new_entities.description: High-dose intravenous ascorbic acid infusions used in wellness, supportive-care, or integrative-medicine settings.

edges.effect_quant: A 141-participant randomized trial in healthy office workers found lower fatigue scores at 2 hours and 1 day after a 10 g IV vitamin C infusion versus saline, while a 39-patient before-after cancer supportive-care study reported lower fatigue and better quality-of-life scores after short-course IV vitamin C. These signals are short-term and population-specific rather than proof of broad, durable anti-fatigue efficacy.
edges.population: adults receiving high-dose IV vitamin C for wellness, supportive care, or symptom-management contexts
edges.mechanism: Potential benefits are typically attributed to transient correction of low vitamin C status, antioxidant effects, and short-lived changes in oxidative stress signaling rather than a disease-specific anti-fatigue mechanism.
edges.summary: This is a mixed supportive-care edge rather than a robust wellness claim. Small human studies suggest some short-term fatigue relief after IV vitamin C, but the evidence base is narrow and does not justify sweeping claims that high-dose infusions reliably fix fatigue.
edges.caveats: Most positive studies are small, short-term, or uncontrolled. Effects seen in fatigued cancer patients or low-vitamin-C subgroups should not be generalized to all consumers seeking IV infusions for energy.

evidence.notes: Intravenous vitamin C administration reduces fatigue in office workers: a double-blind randomized controlled trial.
